items.body_excerpt:
'Our biggest motivation': Top four sides out to follow proven path to premiership
The prospect of a Suncorp Stadium preliminary final is driving the Dolphins as they look to take a big step towards a maiden NRL premiership.
Kristian Woolf's men will travel to Auckland to play the first final in the club's history on Saturday afternoon and they are determined to ensure it's the last time they hit the road before the grand final.
It's the same path the Broncos took to last year's decider, Reece Walsh inspiring a stunning comeback over the Raiders before a thrilling preliminary final victory over the Panthers at a sold-out Suncorp Stadium.
Warriors v Dolphins: Finals Week 1
History shows teams that win a qualifying final in the opening week of the post-season have a much greater chance of playing in the grand final and Dolphins captain Tom Gilbert said his side is determined to swing the odds in their favour this weekend.
"To have the chance to play a preliminary final at our home stadium is our biggest motivation," Gilbert told NRL.com. "It's the same for them, they'll want that as well so there's a lot of motivation there for both sides.
"If we think too far ahead we won't get this weekend right so we're looking forward to the opportunity and challenges that comes with playing in New Zealand and we're going to try enjoy the week."
The top four sides will do battle on either side of the Tasman this weekend, with a week off and a place in the preliminary final on the line.
The Warriors will host the Dolphins at Go Media Stadium on Saturday afternoon before the Panthers take on the Roosters in a CommBank Stadium blockbuster on Sunday.
Gilbert's blessing in disguise
The winners will enjoy a rest while the losers will be thrust into a sudden-death semi-final against the two elimination final winners next weekend.
Statistics provided by rugby league historian David Middleton reveal just how important a win is this week for the four teams contesting qualifying finals.
In every season since the NRL introduced the current finals format in 2012 at least one qualifying final winner has gone on to play in the grand final.
On the flipside, just four top four teams have lost in week one and recovered to progress to the decider.
The 2015 Cowboys and 2021 Panthers are the only two sides to lose a qualifying final before reeling off three-straight victories to claim the premiership.
While they did it the hard way in 2021, Penrith took the more direct route in 2022, 2023 and 2024 by winning in week one and enjoying a week off before the preliminary final.
Panthers v Roosters: Finals Week 1
Having experienced both paths, veteran forward Scott Sorensen said it's crucial his side opens their finals campaign with a win.
"I'm not going to deny how important it is to start the finals on the front foot and perform well," Sorensen said. "You build confidence in that and then have the luxury of a week off to freshen up.
"If we have to do it the hard way or the easy way, we're just as prepared.
"It is tougher if you have to go out there and play for another 80 minutes but at the end of the day, if you lose and want to get there, that's the way you've got to go. You've got to accept it, move on and be excited for the occasion."

NRL Casualty Ward: Walker goes down with calf injury
The Rabbitohs' have been dealt a body blow at Allianz Stadium on Friday night with spiritual leader Cody Walker suffering a calf injury.
Walker collapsed to the turf with no one around him in the 31st minute and immediately signalled to the bench that he was in trouble.
The 36-year-old felt for his calf and hobbled to the sideline where he was visibly distressed as the reality set in that his season looks over.
Walker sat on the bench for the second half with ice on his calf and carrying a crutch.
The Warriors have received a huge boost ahead of their qualifying final against the Dolphins with gun forward Jackson Ford set to return from a pectoral injury.
After making a dynamic start to the season in which he averaged 161 run metres and 41 tackles per game, Ford suffered the injury in Round 16 against the Cowboys and initial fears were he could miss the rest of the year.
Ford has been named on the bench for the blockbuster Go Media Stadium showdown against the Dolphins, who get Selwyn Cobbo (ankle), back-rower Kulikefu Finefeuiaki (knee) and five-eighth Kodi Nikorima (hamstring) back for their first ever final.
Nikorima and Finefeuiaki were given last week off to get over niggling injuries ahead of the finals.
The Roosters also have a star forward returning for their qualifying final against Penrith with Angus Crichton back after 11 games out with a foot injury.
Also back on deck at the Roosters are Victor Radley (concussion) and a posse of stars who were rested in Round 27 including James Tedesco , Daly Cherry-Evans and Rob Toia .
The Rabbitohs have Tallis Duncan back from a hamstring injury but will be without veteran back-rower Euan Aitken for the rest of the season after he fractured his scapula in the win over the Roosters.
The injury is a cruel blow for 31-year-old Aitken, who was on the verge of playing in just the second finals match of his 223-game career.
Aitken's only finals appearance came with the Dragons in his debut season in 2015.

The game was just five minutes old when Tuimalatu-Brown was taken low by Cam McInnes and Michael Gabrael over the top, with the Sharks debutant making high contact.
In an update on Sunday morning , the Storm said initial assessments indicate the youngster does not have a severe spinal injury but he will undergo further testing due to numbness in his arm.
"Siulagi was admitted to hospital overnight after concerns for a neck injury," the statement said. "There was no severe spinal injury on initial assessment but he will undergo further scans today due to concerns for some ongoing numbness to the arm."

Warriors v Dolphins NRL qualifying final: Kick-off time, team list, injuries - everything to know
Caption: Taine Tuaupiki Photo credit: Hannah Peters
NRL qualifying final: Warriors v Dolphins
Kick-off 6pm Saturday,12 September
Go Media Mt Smart Stadium, Auckland
Live blog updates on RNZ.co.nz
While a minor premiership would have been a "cool slice of history" for the Warriors, star Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad says the team's focus is firmly on "the big one" in four weeks.
A top four finish has given the Warriors a massive advantage as they kick off their finals campaign against the Redcliffe Dolphins at Go Media Mt Smart Stadium on Saturday - with home field advantage and essentially an extra life in the first week of the NRL finals series.
"It starts this weekend against a really strong, in-form Dolphins side - we'll focus on that job first and we'll see how we go," Nicoll-Klokstad said.
With only two points separating the sides in their prior two meetings this season, he conceded the team will need to be "on" for the full 80 minutes.
"They've got strike weapons left, right and centre," he said. "They've got speed and Hammer [Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow] at the back."
The competition's dark horses - the Dolphins - will certainly be no easy task for the Warriors, who aren't looking to reinvent themselves.
Both teams have been split down the middle in their short history with five wins and five losses each - and the last seven games between the clubs having been decided by four points or less.
Taine Tuaupiki - who will play at fullback this weekend - said the squad is "doubling down on the simple things" and looking to its leaders who have been through the finals pressure before.
"We've got a young squad, a lot of us haven't played finals footy before, so when the leaders speak, you listen, because they know what's happening," Tuaupiki said.
The Warriors have also shown throughout the season they can find a way to win tight games, something Tuaupiki believes could prove just as important as putting together a dominant performance.
"If we're in a final, if we win this week, by one point, no one's going to be saying anything about their defence. All you're going to know is we won," he said.
"So at the end of the day, that's what we need to do, we just need a win."
The winners of the qualifying finals this weekend will get to leapfrog the next week of the playoffs and get a week off to rest moving straight through to the preliminary finals.
The losers get a lifeline - a second chance - and they play the two winners of the Elimination finals from week one next weekend.
RNZ / LIAM K. SWIGGS
Here's everything to know ahead of Warriors v Dolphins:
History
As the Dolphins enter their first ever finals series in the club's third year in the NRL, they are shaping up to be one of the Warriors' most formidable rivals.
The last seven consecutive meetings dating back to May 2024 have all proved to be absolute blockbusters between the two sides - ending in no less than four-point margins every time.
Their last meeting - in round 17 at Suncorp Stadium - ended in heartbreak when a last-minute Dolphins try sealed the victory 26-24 in one of the games of the season.
But that's not to say the Warriors themselves haven't got the job done before - coming back from a 14-18 half-time deficit in round 8, stealing a victory of their own 20-18 in front of a rare sellout Wellington crowd.
Form
Recent form doesn't indicate much going into Saturday's game with very little separating the two sides.
The Warriors enter week one of the Finals series off the back of a strong six-game winning streak, most recently taking down the Manly Sea Eagles 31-30 with a Chanel Harris-Tavita field goal.
Meanwhile, the Dolphins boast an ever more impressive seven-game winning streak heading into Saturday - even if it only includes one top eight scalp compared to the Warriors three.

Match Preview: Qualifying Final – Dolphins v Warriors
Seven games. Nothing more than four points between them. Now, a place in the preliminary final is on the line.
Since May 2024, every meeting between the Dolphins and Warriors has been decided by either two or four points, and this Saturday the rivalry enters new territory as the Dolphins make their first-ever NRL finals appearance.
The Dolphins head across the Tasman riding seven consecutive victories and carrying plenty of momentum into their qualifying final against the Warriors at Go Media Stadium.
With the winner earning a week off and progressing directly to a home preliminary final, there is more at stake than ever.
The two sides have already met twice in 2026, splitting the honours with one win apiece.
The first came in Round 8 in Wellington, where the Warriors edged out the Dolphins 20–18 in a two-point thriller.
It was a different story when the Warriors travelled to Suncorp Stadium in Round 17, with the Dolphins turning the tables to claim a 26–24 victory.
Jamayne Isaako also enters the clash within reach of another milestone, requiring 12 points to become just the fourth player in premiership history to score 300 points in a season.
Team News
Dolphins
Selwyn Cobbo returns to the wing after missing last week’s final regular-season clash, while Kodi Nikorima slots back into the number six jersey after being rested for Round 27 against the Titans.
Kulikefu Finefeuiaki also returns to the starting side in the second row after being a late withdrawal last week.
Connelly Lemuelu has been named on the interchange bench, while Felise Kaufusi is listed as 18th man.
Jake Averillo, Brian Pouniu and Tevita Naufahu move back to the extended squad
Warriors
The Warriors have received a boost with Jackson Ford named to make his first appearance since Round 16 after recovering from a pectoral injury.
Centre Leka Halasima returns from an ankle injury, while Wayde Egan and Kurt Capewell are also back in the side after being rested last week.
Sam Healey, Adam Pompey and Eddie Ieremia-Toeava move to the extended interchange, with Jett Cleary and Luke Laulilii also included in the extended squad.
Match-Up
James Fisher-Harris v Thomas Flegler
Two powerhouse props. Two different jobs. One massive finals battle.
James Fisher-Harris and Thomas Flegler will collide in the middle in a match-up built for the occasion, with both forwards capable of setting the tone for their side.
A multiple premiership winner, Fisher-Harris knows exactly what finals football demands. The Warriors captain will look to lead from the front, running hard through the middle and challenging the Dolphins’ defensive line with every carry.
For Flegler, the occasion carries a different meaning. After spending an extended period on the sidelines, the Dolphins prop has the opportunity to make his presence felt when it matters most, bringing the physicality and defensive intent that has become crucial to the Dolphins’ run into September.
While Fisher-Harris will look to generate momentum through the middle, Flegler’s job will be to shut it down.
The Dolphins have plenty of strike power in their outside backs to generate metres with the ball, allowing their forwards to conserve valuable energy for the defensive battle through the middle.
That makes stopping Fisher-Harris and the Warriors’ powerful forward pack a key assignment.
One will be looking to lead through his carries. The other will be waiting to meet him.
It’s a heavyweight battle made for finals football.

Finals football returns to Go Media Stadium on Saturday afternoon, and it is difficult to find a better matchup to begin the qualifying final portion of the 2026 NRL Finals Series . The second placed Warriors host the third placed Dolphins , with the winner earning a week off and progressing directly to a home preliminary final. For two clubs chasing their maiden premiership, that is an enormous prize.
This is my game of the week, and the brief history between these teams tells us exactly why. They have already met twice in 2026, with both matches decided by four points or fewer. The Dolphins won 26-24, while the Warriors took the other meeting 20-18.
The market has New Zealand around a converted try favourite, but I see these sides as much more evenly matched. Go Media Stadium is a significant advantage, and the Warriors deserve favouritism, but Dolphins +5.5 gives us valuable protection in a game I expect to be alive deep into the final 10 minutes.
Team news only strengthens the quality of the contest. The Dolphins are genuinely full strength for their first finals appearance, while New Zealand welcome back Wayde Egan, Kurt Capewell, Leka Halasima and Jackson Ford. The Warriors remain without Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, but otherwise have close to their best available side.
Let's break it all down!

New Zealand’s second place finish confirms that 2026 has been far more than another encouraging Warriors season. Andrew Webster’s side has developed into a genuine premiership contender, balancing one of the competition’s strongest forward packs with a defensive structure capable of winning when the attack is not flowing.
The most significant aspect of their year has been resilience. The Warriors dealt with injuries and selection disruption throughout the regular season yet continued finding ways to bank victories. Their defining performance may have been the 28-12 win over Penrith at Go Media Stadium in Round 23, when their forwards physically overwhelmed the ladder leaders and Leka Halasima produced 239 metres and 11 tackle breaks. That victory started an unbeaten run through the final month, with New Zealand subsequently beating Brisbane, South Sydney, Newcastle and Manly on the way to second place.
That forward strength remains their greatest weapon heading into September. James Fisher-Harris and Mitch Barnett form a brutal starting front row combination, while Erin Clark, Jacob Laban and Kurt Capewell give New Zealand mobility and work rate around them. Te Maire Martin and Chanel Harris-Tavita do not possess the star power of some finals halves combinations, but they have enough experience and structure to play off a dominant pack.
The loss of Watene-Zelezniak remains meaningful. He provides elite finishing and yardage from his own end, and his collarbone injury removes one of New Zealand’s most reliable attacking weapons. Still, this team has spent the entire year proving its system can absorb personnel changes.
Now comes the real test. The Warriors have not hosted a finals match since beating Newcastle 40-10 in 2023 and Go Media Stadium should be deafening. Webster targets 'simple fixes' as Wahs tune up for tilt at history
After riding the highs of a preliminary final in his first year at the helm and the lows of a 13th-place finish in his second, Andrew Webster believes his side is better equipped than ever to deliver the Warriors' maiden premiership.
The Wahs have emerged as one of the premiership heavyweights in 2026, finishing second on the ladder with an 18-6 record and earning a home qualifying final against the Dolphins.
For Webster, it is another opportunity to chase the ultimate prize in his third crack at finals footy in four years at the helm in Auckland.
Webster knows his side have shown some minor defensive lapses in recent weeks, but rather than hitting the panic button, he sees them as problems that are ‘simple fixes’ and what could be a secret weapon.
“We are going after teams. We will make it hard for them and we need to iron out one little thing. If you didn't have that piece of improvement, you can come into the finals complacent," Webster said.
“The biggest thing for me around it is that it’s an easy fix, it’s a simple fix."
The Warriors faithful are up and about!
That calmness has become a Webster trademark - a trait he no doubt honed while working alongside Ivan Cleary during the Panthers' glory run.
Webster was Cleary's assistant coach in back-to-back premierships in 2021 and 2022, gaining a first-hand look at the standards required to consistently perform in September.
Now he is trying to create those same habits in Auckland.
“Making sure each rep counts, each moment your focus is on that. If you have a good training session, it gives you a good chance to have a good game," said Webster.
“I’ll repeat myself 100 times, making sure we don’t turn up on game day and try to be something we’re not.
“We know what our footy looks like. We don’t mind if someone else knows, and the opposition knows what we look like.
“We’ll be at our best and do it our way. We are confident.”
That belief will be put to the test against the Dolphins, with the Warriors playing in front of a sold-out Go Media Stadium and their loyal home support that has become such a weapon throughout the whole season.
Super Saiyan Laban gets two
But while the occasion will be big, Webster is determined not to let his players get caught up in it.
“Everyone’s really level-headed, grounded, knows what they’ve got to do. We’re very big on being ourselves,” he said.
“We have a lot of experience, a lot of confidence, a lot of players that we believe in.
“Bring your best football and the rest takes care of itself.”
And Webster knows the Warriors will need leadership from inside the playing group when the game heats up.
Webster: 'Everyone's really level-headed, grounded'
Enter four-time premiership winning prop James Fisher-Harris and NSW Origin hardman Mitch Barnett, who have formed a formidable co-captaincy pairing.
“They are big games with lots of pressure and we are in a good spot that has a balance of that youth who aren’t scared or intimidated by it because they don’t know it yet, then you have those guys who have been there a lot and know exactly what to do,” he said.
“We could not be more wrapped than those two as captains. We are so happy they are ours.
“They take it upon themselves to not assume the boys aren’t ready on game day and they’ve got some great supporters around them.”

Fit and firing forward pack a key factor in Phins finals push
Dolphins forwards Ray Stone and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki count the lessons learnt and a fully fit forward pack as key reasons why the squad is primed to surprise in their maiden finals campaign.
Having helped the side achieve their finals goal in his final season with the club; the retiring Stone said one major factor to their success so far this season had been a relative good health of their forward pack, despite losing Daniel Saifiti to medical retirement earlier this year.
Ray Stone on the charge for the Dolphins. ©Zain Mohammed / NRL Images
Last season, Stone was forced to play through AC joint sprains, getting weekly needles in both shoulders as an injury crisis struck the club, with players like Tom Flegler and Tom Gilbert sidelined.
“I think our whole squad's been a lot more healthy, which has definitely helped the middle rotation,” Stone said.
“Last year, I think pretty much our whole start pack was in rehab, so being a lot healthier this year, the minutes have been distributed a lot differently, which has helped me keep my body a lot fresher.
“I think every pre-season, we've had the squad to do it (make the finals) … I think we could have done it earlier if we had have been healthy those years.
“It's good to see that our whole squad's been healthy this year and we're really pushing on that potential we've got.”
Gilbert's blessing in disguise
For rising forward Finefeuiaki, the feeling around the club was “pretty high”, but the players were focused on the task ahead, taking on an in-form Warriors side in front of their home fans.
Although they finished third on the ladder, the club also suffered some of the worst losses in their history, with two especially poor showings in front of their fans at their spiritual home in Redcliffe - 52-18 against the Sea Eagles and 66-0 against Cronulla - providing an opportunity to grow.
“I want to be part of history,” Finefeuiaki said.
“For the club to play their first finals, it's pretty special, not just for me but for the team that we have as well.
“I think we took a lot of lessons from those games that we could have won and the games that we got blown out of the park; those ones have made us come together more and work more on our defence.
Kulikefu Finefeuiaki runs the ball for the Dolphins. ©NRL Images
“I think our defence was the thing that we needed to work because our attack is probably one of the best attacks in that we can score from anywhere if we wanted to …
“We came together as one and just to work together on that (our defence), so for us to secure that top four spot and … a chance to go straight to the prelims this weekend, (that would) be pretty special.
During the regular season, the Dolphins and the Warriors claimed one win apiece, with a combined margin of four points the difference between them.
However, despite the Warriors having the home crowd and more finals experience behind them, the New Zealand-born Finefeuiaki was looking forward to the challenge of upsetting the pride of Aotearoa.

“We're pretty loud, but I don't know if we'll be able to hear each other on the field, but I think that's what we've got to embrace as a team.
“I reckon it'll be one of the best venues to play and to be a part of too.
“I know that it will be a physical game this weekend against the Warriors; I know our boys will be up for it and I know that they'll be up for it too.”

Warriors fans furious as tickets being re-sold for hundreds more
Warriors fans who snapped up tickets to Saturday's NRL finals qualifier match through unofficial resale sites could find their tickets cancelled, Ticketmaster has warned.
Tickets for the clash with the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium sold out within minutes of going on sale to the general public on Tuesday.
Not long afterwards, listings began appearing on TradeMe and other online marketplaces, with some sellers asking hundreds of dollars more than what they paid.
One listing offered four tickets in the Eastern Stand for a buy-now price of $1200, describing them as "arguably the best seats in the house. Right where the Warriors walk out".
The seller did not offer an explanation for why they were selling the tickets.
Another seller was asking $500 for two tickets in the uncovered South Stand - seats which ordinarily cost $25 for an adult during the regular season, although the price for the play-off was increased to around $45.
For some fans, the practice crossed a line. The question-and-answer sections of some listings became impromptu battlegrounds, with frustrated supporters accusing sellers of cashing in on the huge demand for one of the biggest Warriors games in years.
"You're a dog for selling these tickets to make money and actual fans can't even go to see it live," one person wrote.
"You are an actual scumbag," another posted.
Others questioned whether the practice of on-selling the tickets at large mark-up breached the terms and conditions set by Ticketmaster, the official ticketing agent for the game.
In a statement to RNZ, a Ticketmaster spokesperson recommended fans only purchase tickets through authorised ticket sellers.
"Ticketmaster does not guarantee the authenticity of tickets purchased from unauthorised third-party resellers or resale sites.
"While only a relatively small number of tickets appear to have been listed for resale, the NRL's ticket terms restrict unauthorised resale for the Warriors game.
"Tickets identified as sold or transferred in breach of those terms may be cancelled."

"There's always going to be somewhere that's going to take advantage of that sort of stuff but yes you know, they're trying to make money, whereas we just want to watch the game."

Martin retired in 2020 following five years at the Panthers and Cowboys after scans revealed a small brain bleed was causing the continual headaches he was suffering.

“It's our fourth year in the comp and we've got a good group of boys… 100 per cent (the team can make an impact).
"You look across the park and what type of players we do have and the calibre that we have as well, it's pretty scary.
“I think teams do see that, but it doesn't get talked about that much, but if we just stick to ourselves, we know what type of players we have and what we can do within this competition.
“The goal is to get to that grand final and win it and I'm confident that each week we take and each week we improve, we can win it.
“(But) the coaching staff around us, they do keep us grounded.
“We're a pretty happy bunch too and next week's a whole new competition.”

Confidence and believe might be high, but after having to once again come from behind to secure a close win over the Titans, Tabuai-Fidow conceded there was still work to do.
“We'll go back to the drawing board and we'll start all over again and go again,” the Queensland and Samoa representative said.
“I think it's more fine-tuning and what we can do within ourselves, within the team.
“It’s not so much changing anything, we know what type of footy we want to play and we know we could go a long way with the footy we do play.
“It's just fine-tuning some things and just having that week as a stepping stone to a new competition.
“We have all got to step up and I think that's the main thing, just stepping up and fine-tuning and working on what we can improve on.”
